Esther 1.summary: In his third year, King Ahasuerus, who rules 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia, shows off his riches for 180 days and then holds a seven-day feast at Shushan (Esther 1:1–8). Queen Vashti holds a feast for the women (Esther 1:9). When the king is "merry with wine," he sends for Vashti to show her beauty, but she refuses to come, and he is very angry (Esther 1:10–12). Memucan warns that other wives will despise their husbands and advises that Vashti never again come before the king (Esther 1:13–20). The king sends letters to every province "that every man should bear rule in his own house" (Esther 1:21–22).
Esther 1.whereWeAre: Nehemiah ended with the people back in Jerusalem, still struggling to stay faithful. Esther goes back a few decades to Jews who stayed in Persia, starting at King Ahasuerus' feast in Shushan, where Queen Vashti refuses his summons and loses her crown. In chapter 2 the king looks for a new queen.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: King of Persia, who holds a great feast and removes Vashti in anger.

keyFigures.name: Vashti
keyFigures.role: The queen, who refuses to come at the king's command.

keyFigures.name: Memucan
keyFigures.role: One of the king's princes, who advises that Vashti be removed.

keyFigures.name: The seven chamberlains
keyFigures.role: Sent to bring Vashti before the king.

keyThemes.explanation: The king's pride, stirred by wine, leads to anger and a hasty decree.
One queen's refusal becomes a law sent to every province.
Vashti's removal opens the way for Esther to become queen.

Esther 2.summary: The king's servants suggest gathering young women from every province so the king can choose a new queen (Esther 2:1–4). Mordecai, a Benjamite at Shushan, has raised his cousin Hadassah, or Esther, and she is taken into the house of the women under Hegai (Esther 2:5–9). At Mordecai's word, Esther does not tell anyone her people, and Mordecai checks on her every day (Esther 2:10–11). After twelve months of preparation the women go in to the king one by one (Esther 2:12–14). The king loves Esther above all the women and sets the royal crown on her head in his seventh year (Esther 2:15–18). Mordecai learns that Bigthan and Teresh plan to kill the king, Esther tells the king in Mordecai's name, and it is written in the chronicles (Esther 2:19–23).
Esther 2.whereWeAre: Vashti was removed in chapter 1. Now young women are gathered for the king, and Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, is made queen without telling anyone her people. Mordecai saves the king's life, and in chapter 3 a new enemy rises.

keyFigures.name: Esther
keyFigures.role: A Jewish orphan, also called Hadassah, who becomes queen.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.role: Esther's cousin, who raised her and uncovers a plot against the king.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: Loves Esther above all the women and makes her queen.

keyFigures.name: Hegai
keyFigures.role: Keeper of the women, who shows Esther favor.

keyFigures.name: Bigthan and Teresh
keyFigures.role: Two chamberlains who plot to kill the king and are hanged.

keyThemes.explanation: Esther keeps her people secret at Mordecai's word.
Esther wins the favor of Hegai, of all who see her, and of the king.
Mordecai's report is written down and forgotten until chapter 6.

Esther 3.summary: The king promotes Haman the Agagite, and all bow to him, "But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence" (Esther 3:1–4). Haman is full of wrath and plans to destroy not only Mordecai but all the Jews in the kingdom (Esther 3:5–6). In the first month they cast Pur, the lot, before Haman, and it falls on the month Adar (Esther 3:7). Haman tells the king a certain people does not keep his laws and offers ten thousand talents of silver to have them destroyed (Esther 3:8–9). The king gives Haman his ring, and letters go out to kill all the Jews on the thirteenth of Adar (Esther 3:10–14). The king and Haman sit down to drink, "but the city Shushan was perplexed" (Esther 3:15).
Esther 3.whereWeAre: Esther became queen and Mordecai foiled a plot against the king in chapter 2. Now Haman is promoted, Mordecai will not bow to him, and Haman wins a decree to destroy all the Jews. In chapter 4 Mordecai asks Esther to go to the king.

keyFigures.name: Haman
keyFigures.role: Son of Hammedatha the Agagite, who plots to destroy all the Jews.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.role: Refuses to bow to Haman.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: Gives Haman his ring and lets him send the decree.

keyFigures.name: The king's servants
keyFigures.role: Ask Mordecai daily why he will not bow, then tell Haman.

keyThemes.explanation: Mordecai will not give Haman the honor the king commanded.
Haman's anger at one man becomes a plan to destroy a whole people.
Haman tells the king a twisted story to get his decree.

Esther 4.summary: Mordecai tears his clothes and cries out in sackcloth, and in every province the Jews mourn and fast (Esther 4:1–3). Esther sends Hatach to find out why, and Mordecai sends her a copy of the decree and asks her to plead with the king (Esther 4:4–9). Esther answers that anyone who goes to the king uncalled will die unless he holds out the golden sceptre, and he has not called her for thirty days (Esther 4:10–12). Mordecai warns that she will not escape and asks, "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:13–14). Esther tells the Jews in Shushan to fast three days and says, "if I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:15–17).
Esther 4.whereWeAre: Haman's decree went out in chapter 3. Now the Jews mourn, and Mordecai tells Esther she may have come to the kingdom "for such a time as this" (Esther 4:14). Esther calls a fast and, in chapter 5, goes to the king uninvited.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.role: Mourns in sackcloth and urges Esther to go to the king.

keyFigures.name: Esther
keyFigures.role: Calls a fast and decides to risk her life.

keyFigures.name: Hatach
keyFigures.role: The chamberlain who carries messages between Esther and Mordecai.

keyFigures.name: The Jews
keyFigures.role: Mourn in every province and fast with Esther in Shushan.

keyThemes.explanation: The Jews answer the decree with mourning, fasting, and weeping.

keyThemes.theme: For such a time as this
keyThemes.explanation: Mordecai suggests that Esther became queen for this very purpose.
Esther chooses to go to the king though it may cost her life.

Esther 5.summary: On the third day Esther stands in the inner court, and the king holds out the golden sceptre to her (Esther 5:1–2). He offers her up to half the kingdom, but she only invites him and Haman to a banquet (Esther 5:3–5). At the banquet she invites them to a second banquet the next day (Esther 5:6–8). Haman leaves joyful, but when Mordecai will not stand up for him, he is full of anger (Esther 5:9). He boasts to his friends and his wife Zeresh, yet says, "all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate" (Esther 5:10–13). Zeresh and his friends tell him to build a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai, and he does (Esther 5:14).
Esther 5.whereWeAre: Esther decided to risk her life in chapter 4. Now the king holds out his sceptre to her, and she invites him and Haman to a banquet, while Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai. In chapter 6 a sleepless night changes everything.

keyFigures.name: Esther
keyFigures.role: Goes to the king uncalled and invites him and Haman to a banquet.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: Holds out the golden sceptre and offers Esther up to half the kingdom.

keyFigures.name: Haman
keyFigures.role: Boasts of his honor but is enraged by Mordecai and builds a gallows.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.role: Will not stand up or move for Haman at the gate.

keyFigures.name: Zeresh
keyFigures.role: Haman's wife, who with his friends advises the gallows.

keyThemes.explanation: Esther waits for the right moment instead of rushing her request.
Haman has wealth and honor, yet one man's refusal spoils it all.
Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai.

Esther 6.summary: "On that night could not the king sleep," so the chronicles are read to him, and he hears how Mordecai saved his life (Esther 6:1–2). He learns that nothing was done to honor Mordecai (Esther 6:3). Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's death, and the king asks him, "What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour?" (Esther 6:4–6). Thinking the king means him, Haman suggests the king's robe, horse, and crown and a noble to lead him through the city (Esther 6:7–9). The king tells Haman to do it for Mordecai, and Haman leads Mordecai through the street (Esther 6:10–11). Haman hurries home mourning, his wife says he will surely fall before Mordecai, and the king's servants rush him to the banquet (Esther 6:12–14).
Esther 6.whereWeAre: Haman built a gallows for Mordecai in chapter 5. That night the king cannot sleep, learns that Mordecai saved his life, and makes Haman lead Mordecai through the city in honor. In chapter 7 Haman goes to Esther's second banquet.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: Cannot sleep, hears of Mordecai's deed, and orders him honored.

keyFigures.name: Haman
keyFigures.role: Plans his own honor and is made to give it to Mordecai.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.role: Rides through the city in the king's robe.

keyFigures.name: Zeresh
keyFigures.role: Tells Haman he will surely fall before Mordecai.

keyThemes.explanation: A sleepless night and a book of records bring Mordecai's deed to light.
Haman plans his own honor and must give it to his enemy.
Haman's own family sees that he will fall before Mordecai.

Esther 7.summary: At the second banquet the king again offers Esther whatever she asks (Esther 7:1–2). She asks for her life and her people's, "For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed" (Esther 7:3–4). When the king asks who has done this, she says, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman" (Esther 7:5–6). The king goes out in anger, and when he returns, Haman has fallen on Esther's couch begging for his life (Esther 7:7–8). Harbonah tells of the gallows Haman built for Mordecai, and "they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai" (Esther 7:9–10).
Esther 7.whereWeAre: Haman was forced to honor Mordecai in chapter 6. Now, at the second banquet, Esther reveals that she is a Jew and names Haman as the enemy, and he is hanged on his own gallows. Chapter 8 deals with the decree that is still in force.

keyFigures.name: Esther
keyFigures.role: Pleads for her people and names Haman as their enemy.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: Orders Haman hanged on his own gallows.

keyFigures.name: Haman
keyFigures.role: Exposed at the banquet and put to death.

keyFigures.name: Harbonah
keyFigures.role: A chamberlain who tells the king about Haman's gallows.

keyThemes.explanation: Esther reveals her people and asks for their lives.
Haman dies on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
The man who planned murder is exposed and judged.

Esther 8.summary: The king gives Haman's house to Esther and his ring to Mordecai, and Esther sets Mordecai over Haman's house (Esther 8:1–2). Esther falls at the king's feet and begs him to reverse Haman's letters (Esther 8:3–6). Since a writing sealed with the king's ring cannot be reversed, the king tells Esther and Mordecai to write a new one in his name (Esther 8:7–8). The new letters let the Jews in every city gather and stand for their lives on the thirteenth of Adar (Esther 8:9–14). Mordecai goes out in royal apparel, "The Jews had light, and gladness, and joy, and honour," and many people become Jews (Esther 8:15–17).
Esther 8.whereWeAre: Haman died in chapter 7, but his decree could not be reversed. Now Mordecai receives the king's ring and sends a new decree letting the Jews defend themselves. In chapter 9 the day of the decree arrives.

keyFigures.name: Esther
keyFigures.role: Begs the king to stop Haman's plan.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.role: Receives the king's ring and writes the new decree.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: Lets Esther and Mordecai write in his name.

keyFigures.name: The Jews
keyFigures.role: Rejoice at the new decree in every province.

keyThemes.explanation: Esther, now safe herself, still begs for her people.

keyThemes.theme: A way through an unchangeable law
keyThemes.explanation: The first decree stands, but a second lets the Jews defend themselves.
The Jews have light, gladness, joy, and honour.

Esther 9.summary: On the thirteenth of Adar, the day their enemies hoped to rule them, the Jews gather and no one can stand against them (Esther 9:1–2). The rulers of the provinces help the Jews because they fear Mordecai (Esther 9:3–4). In Shushan the Jews kill five hundred men and Haman's ten sons, "but on the spoil laid they not their hand" (Esther 9:5–10). At Esther's request, the Jews in Shushan are given a second day, and Haman's sons are hanged (Esther 9:11–15). In the provinces the Jews kill seventy-five thousand of their foes, take no spoil, and rest and feast (Esther 9:16–19). Mordecai sends letters to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar each year, with feasting and "gifts to the poor" (Esther 9:20–22). The days are called Purim, after Pur, and Esther confirms them with a second letter (Esther 9:23–32).
Esther 9.whereWeAre: Mordecai's new decree went out in chapter 8. On the thirteenth of Adar the Jews defeat those who attack them, and Mordecai and Esther set up the yearly feast of Purim. Chapter 10 closes with Mordecai's greatness.

keyFigures.name: The Jews
keyFigures.role: Gather on the thirteenth of Adar and stand for their lives.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.role: Grows great and sends letters setting up Purim.

keyFigures.name: Esther
keyFigures.role: Asks for a second day in Shushan and confirms Purim by letter.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: Grants Esther's request.

keyFigures.name: The rulers of the provinces
keyFigures.role: Help the Jews because they fear Mordecai.

keyThemes.explanation: The day meant for the Jews' destruction becomes the day they rule over their enemies.
Three times the text says the Jews did not take the spoil.
Purim is kept every year so no generation forgets.
The feast includes gifts to one another and to the poor.

Esther 10.summary: Ahasuerus lays a tribute on the land and the isles of the sea (Esther 10:1). His acts and Mordecai's greatness are written in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia (Esther 10:2). Mordecai is "next unto king Ahasuerus," great among the Jews, "seeking the wealth of his people, and speaking peace to all his seed" (Esther 10:3).
Esther 10.whereWeAre: The Jews were saved and Purim was set up in chapter 9. This short chapter records Mordecai's greatness as second only to the king. Job follows, beginning the books of poetry and wisdom with a righteous man who suffers.

keyFigures.name: Ahasuerus
keyFigures.role: Lays a tribute on the land and the isles.

keyFigures.name: Mordecai
keyFigures.role: Second to the king, seeking the good of his people.

keyThemes.explanation: Mordecai, once marked for death, is second only to the king.
Mordecai uses his power for the wealth and peace of his people.
Mordecai's greatness is written in the royal chronicles.
